data.name: Cutting_Lead
data.value: A cutting is a piece of stem that grows its own roots and becomes a new plant. Most climbing and trailing houseplants, like pothos, philodendron and tradescantia, root easily this way.
data.comment: Guide, taking a cutting: the lead paragraph.

data.name: Cutting_WhenTitle
data.value: When

data.name: Cutting_When
data.value: Cuttings root fastest in late spring and early summer, while the plant is growing, but they root at most times of year. Many growers find rooting slower in a cool room.
data.comment: Guide, taking a cutting: when to take one.

data.name: Cutting_Need
data.value: Clean, sharp scissors or a knife, and a glass, pot or box for what it roots in.
data.comment: Guide, taking a cutting: what to have ready.

data.name: Cutting_Step1
data.value: Pick a healthy stem the plant can spare, with no pests on it.

data.name: Cutting_Step2
data.value: Find the nodes: the joints where a leaf meets the stem, often with a bump or a small brown root. Roots grow from the nodes.

data.name: Cutting_Step3
data.value: Cut just below a node, so the piece is about 8 to 10 cm long with two or more nodes. A tip cutting usually roots fastest.

data.name: Cutting_Step4
data.value: Take off the lower leaves and any flowers, and keep 2 or 3 leaves at the top. Leaves that would sit in water or compost rot there.

data.name: Cutting_Step5
data.value: For succulents, cacti, pelargoniums and rubber plants, leave the cut end to dry and seal for a day or so first.

data.name: Cutting_Step6
data.value: Rooting powder is optional. Some sources dip the end in it, others don't use it, and easy plants like pothos root well without.

data.name: Cutting_RootIn
data.value: Root it in
data.comment: Guide, taking a cutting: label over the choice of what to root in.

data.name: Cutting_Water
data.value: Water
data.comment: Guide, taking a cutting: name of a method.

data.name: Cutting_Mix
data.value: Cutting mix
data.comment: Guide, taking a cutting: name of a method.

data.name: Cutting_Sphagnum
data.value: Sphagnum moss
data.comment: Guide, taking a cutting: name of a method.

data.name: Cutting_WaterWhy
data.value: You can see the roots come, and it needs nothing but a glass. Many growers pick it for that.
data.comment: Guide, taking a cutting, water: why people pick it.

data.name: Cutting_WaterSteps
data.value: Stand the cutting in water with a node under the surface and the leaves above it. Keep it in a bright spot out of direct sun. Change the water every few days so it stays clean.
data.comment: Guide, taking a cutting, water: steps.

data.name: Cutting_WaterHowLong
data.value: About 10 days for the easiest, 3 to 4 weeks for most.
data.comment: Guide, taking a cutting, water: how long.

data.name: Cutting_WaterWinter
data.value: In winter, when cuttings root slowly, they may rot in water before they root, and a mix does better.
data.comment: Guide, taking a cutting, water: a note about winter.

data.name: Cutting_WaterWatch
data.value: Cloudy or smelly water and a soft brown stem end mean rot. Many growers cut above it and start again in fresh water. Roots grown in water are used to water, so the move to compost is the risky part. See Potting it up.
data.comment: Guide, taking a cutting, water: what to watch for.

data.name: Cutting_MixWhy
data.value: The roots grow in what the plant will live in, so there is no move from water to compost. Many growers pick it for that.
data.comment: Guide, taking a cutting, mix: why people pick it.

data.name: Cutting_MixSteps
data.value: Fill a small pot with half peat-free multipurpose compost and half perlite, or equal parts peat and perlite, vermiculite or sand. Make a hole with a pencil, set the cutting in so a node is buried and the leaves sit just above the surface, and water well.
data.comment: Guide, taking a cutting, mix: steps.

data.name: Cutting_MixKeep
data.value: Keep the mix moist but not soggy. A clear bag over the pot, or a clear box or jar, keeps the air around it damp. Keep it out of direct sun, which heats it up. Some growers open the cover now and then for air.
data.comment: Guide, taking a cutting, mix: keeping it damp.

data.name: Cutting_MixHowLong
data.value: 1 to 2 weeks for soft stems, about 3 to 4 weeks for most. Many growers read a gentle tug that meets resistance as roots.
data.comment: Guide, taking a cutting, mix: how long.

data.name: Cutting_MixWatch
data.value: Mould on the surface or a blackened stem, which many growers put down to too wet a mix or too little air.
data.comment: Guide, taking a cutting, mix: what to watch for.

data.name: Cutting_SphagnumWhy
data.value: It holds water and air at the same time, and many growers use it for aroids and hoyas.
data.comment: Guide, taking a cutting, sphagnum: why people pick it.

data.name: Cutting_SphagnumSteps
data.value: Wet the moss and put it in a clear cup, enough to cover the base of the cutting. Push the cutting gently in and cover the cup with plastic that doesn't touch the leaves. Keep it in bright light out of direct sun, and add water if the moss dries. Many growers squeeze the moss until it no longer drips.
data.comment: Guide, taking a cutting, sphagnum: steps.

data.name: Cutting_SphagnumHowLong
data.value: About a month.
data.comment: Guide, taking a cutting, sphagnum: how long.

data.name: Cutting_SphagnumGloves
data.value: Wear gloves: a rare skin infection has been linked to sphagnum moss, and a mask is advised when handling it dry.
data.comment: Guide, taking a cutting, sphagnum: a safety note.

data.name: Cutting_SphagnumWatch
data.value: Moss kept dripping wet, which many growers say rots the stem.
data.comment: Guide, taking a cutting, sphagnum: what to watch for.

data.name: Cutting_PotTitle
data.value: Potting it up

data.name: Cutting_PotLead
data.value: Sources differ on how long to wait, and both ways are common:
data.comment: Guide, taking a cutting: line before the two ways to pot up.

data.name: Cutting_PotEarly
data.value: Early: pot it up once the roots are about 2.5 cm long, since short roots settle into compost more easily. Many growers say the same.
data.comment: Guide, taking a cutting: the early way to pot up.

data.name: Cutting_PotLater
data.value: Later: wait for a good set of roots and new growth before potting up.
data.comment: Guide, taking a cutting: the later way to pot up.

data.name: Cutting_PotHow
data.value: Pot each one into a small pot, 8 to 10 cm, of peat-free multipurpose compost. Some growers keep the compost a little moister than usual for the first week or two while the roots get used to it. Others add a spoonful of compost to the water over a few days before the move.
data.comment: Guide, taking a cutting: how to pot up.

data.name: Cutting_InApp
data.value: Mark the propagation Rooting when the first root shows and Rooted when it is ready, and Pot up when it goes into a pot. The days it took are then counted for you.
data.comment: Guide, taking a cutting: how it works in the app. Uses the names of the stages.

data.name: SemiHydro_Lead
data.value: In semi-hydro a plant grows in clay pebbles (LECA) or a mix of mineral grains like PON instead of soil, and drinks from water that stands at the bottom of the pot and that the pebbles soak up. The pebbles give off almost no nutrients, so the water carries the feed. The move from soil can be tricky, and rotting roots are the main risk.
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro: the lead paragraph.

data.name: SemiHydro_Where
data.value: No horticultural society or university has written about moving a houseplant from soil to semi-hydro. This guide is how growers and the makers of PON and hydroculture fertiliser describe it, and a line that only growers stand behind says so.
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro: why the sources are thin. Shown under the lead.

data.name: SemiHydro_WhichTitle
data.value: Which plants

data.name: SemiHydro_Which
data.value: Young plants and cuttings make the move most easily. An old plant that has grown in soil for years finds it harder. Robust plants like pothos, spider plant and peace lily are the easiest to start with. Some growers find that plants that like to dry out between waterings do less well with water always at their roots.
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro: which plants move best.

data.name: SemiHydro_Need1
data.value: LECA or PON.
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro: what to have ready.

data.name: SemiHydro_Need2
data.value: A pot with holes inside a pot without holes, or a self-watering pot, so the water stands below the roots. Many growers set it up this way.
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro: what to have ready.

data.name: SemiHydro_Need3
data.value: A fertiliser made for hydroculture, since the pebbles give off almost no nutrients.
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro: what to have ready.

data.name: SemiHydro_Need4
data.value: An opaque pot, since light on the water grows algae, as many growers say.
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro: what to have ready.

data.name: SemiHydro_ReadyTitle
data.value: Get the medium ready

data.name: SemiHydro_Ready
data.value: Rinse LECA until the water runs clear, to wash off the clay dust. Many growers soak it for a few hours too. Some growers rinse PON, others use it straight from the bag.
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro: getting the pebbles ready.

data.name: SemiHydro_Step1
data.value: Take the plant out of its pot.

data.name: SemiHydro_Step2
data.value: Get all the soil off the roots. Many growers soak the root ball in a bowl of water first to loosen it, then work it loose with their fingers and rinse. Soil left between the pebbles packs down and rots, and some fine roots break off.

data.name: SemiHydro_Step3
data.value: Trim any soft, brown or rotten roots.

data.name: SemiHydro_Step4
data.value: Set the plant in the new pot and fill around the roots with the pebbles, at the depth it stood before, as many growers do.

data.name: SemiHydro_SetupTitle
data.value: Two ways to set up the pot

data.name: SemiHydro_Setup
data.value: The pot of pebbles can stand in the water, or stand above it with a wick drawing the water up. Many growers use each. The wick way has its own guide:
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro: before the link to the wick guide.

data.name: SemiHydro_HowMove
data.value: How to move it
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro: label over the choice of how to move.

data.name: SemiHydro_Straight
data.value: Straight in
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro: name of a method.

data.name: SemiHydro_WaterFirst
data.value: Water roots first
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro: name of a method.

data.name: SemiHydro_Lechuza
data.value: Soil over PON (LECHUZA's way)
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro: name of a method.

data.name: SemiHydro_StraightWhy
data.value: One step, and the plant keeps its roots. Many growers pick it for that.
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro, straight in: why people pick it.

data.name: SemiHydro_StraightHow
data.value: Move it straight into the pebbles after washing. Many growers keep the water low at first, just touching the bottom of the pebbles, and change it often.
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro, straight in: how.

data.name: SemiHydro_StraightWatch
data.value: Many growers see the old soil roots die back over the first weeks while new white water roots grow. Some leaves may yellow.
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro, straight in: what to watch for.

data.name: SemiHydro_WaterFirstWhy
data.value: The plant grows roots made for water before it goes into the pebbles, so less dies back, as many growers describe it.
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro, water roots first: why people pick it.

data.name: SemiHydro_WaterFirstHow
data.value: After washing, stand the roots in water, change it every few days, and move the plant into the pebbles once new white roots have grown. Some growers use this mostly for small plants and cuttings.
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro, water roots first: how.

data.name: SemiHydro_WaterFirstWatch
data.value: The same rot signs as in a glass: cloudy water and soft brown roots.
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro, water roots first: what to watch for.

data.name: SemiHydro_LechuzaWhy
data.value: It is how LECHUZA, the maker of PON, tells you to start a plant in its planters.
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro, soil over PON: why people pick it.

data.name: SemiHydro_LechuzaHow
data.value: LECHUZA's planters hold a layer of PON under potting soil, and the plant is set in the soil. For the first 3 months it is watered from above while the roots grow down, and only then does it drink from the reservoir. This is not a move to PON alone.
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro, soil over PON: how.

data.name: SemiHydro_LechuzaWatch
data.value: LECHUZA says to refill the reservoir only once its indicator reads min, after a dry phase of about 1 week for small plants and 2 for larger ones.
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro, soil over PON: what to watch for.

data.name: SemiHydro_LevelTitle
data.value: The water level

data.name: SemiHydro_LevelLead
data.value: Growers keep it at different heights, and all of these are common:
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro: line before the water levels.

data.name: SemiHydro_Level1
data.value: About a third of the pot's height, say many growers.
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro: a water level.

data.name: SemiHydro_Level2
data.value: Just touching the bottom of the pebbles, so they wick the water up, say some growers.
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro: a water level.

data.name: SemiHydro_Level3
data.value: Some growers let the reservoir run empty for a few days before filling it again, so the roots get air. LECHUZA's instructions do the same, with a dry phase of about 1 to 2 weeks before each refill. Others top it up so the level stays the same.
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro: a water level.

data.name: SemiHydro_LevelNever
data.value: COMPO says the water shouldn't reach where the stem meets the roots, and that the plant shouldn't stand in water all the time.
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro: a limit on the water level.

data.name: SemiHydro_SettlesTitle
data.value: While it settles

data.name: SemiHydro_Settle1
data.value: Change the water and flush the pebbles with fresh water, rather than only topping up, so the roots get oxygen and salts don't build up. Once new roots are growing, COMPO and many growers do it every week or two.
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro: while it settles.

data.name: SemiHydro_Settle2
data.value: Feed: COMPO, a maker of hydroculture fertiliser, says a weak feed each week while the plant is growing. Some growers start straight away, others wait until new roots show.
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro: while it settles.

data.name: SemiHydro_Settle3
data.value: It takes weeks to months before new roots and a new leaf show, say many growers.
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro: while it settles.

data.name: SemiHydro_Settle4
data.value: Watch for: a sour smell, soft brown roots, or a white crust of salts on the pebbles, as many growers put it.
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro: while it settles.

data.name: SemiHydro_InApp
data.value: Moving to semi-hydro is in the More menu on a plant's page. The tracking card then asks for Roots washed, First new water root and First new leaf, and Today asks for a look if nothing happens for a while.
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro: how it works in the app. Uses the names of the tracking steps.

data.name: Wick_Lead
data.value: In a wick pot the plant's pot stands above a reservoir of water, and a cord runs from the water up into the mix. The water climbs the cord the way it climbs a strip of kitchen paper, and the mix takes up what it can hold. It works with soil and with semi-hydro, and many growers use it to water less often or while they are away.
data.comment: Guide, watering through a wick: the lead paragraph.

data.name: Wick_WetTitle
data.value: How wet it gets
data.comment: Guide, watering through a wick: heading.

data.name: Wick_Wet
data.value: The wick can't make the mix wetter than the mix itself holds. A mix that holds a lot of water stays too wet in a wick pot, which is why the mix matters more than the wick. A thicker wick only brings the water faster, so a big pot needs a thicker wick or more than one.
data.comment: Guide, watering through a wick: how wet the mix gets.

data.name: Wick_Need1
data.value: A pot with a hole in the bottom, and a container for the water that the pot can stand on or in without touching the water. Some self-watering pots come with both.
data.comment: Guide, watering through a wick: what to have ready.

data.name: Wick_Need2
data.value: A wick of synthetic cord, like nylon or acrylic yarn, or a strip of nylon stocking. Cotton and wool rot in the wet, and many growers avoid them.
data.comment: Guide, watering through a wick: what to have ready.

data.name: Wick_Step1
data.value: Thread the wick through the hole in the bottom of the pot, so a few centimetres lie along the bottom inside and the rest hangs below.
data.comment: Guide, watering through a wick: step 1.

data.name: Wick_Step2
data.value: Many growers wet the wick through before they start, so the water starts climbing at once.
data.comment: Guide, watering through a wick: step 2.

data.name: Wick_Step3
data.value: Fill the pot with the mix and the plant, with the wick lying at the bottom. A wick pushed up into the middle makes the middle wetter.
data.comment: Guide, watering through a wick: step 3.

data.name: Wick_Step4
data.value: Fill the container with water and stand the pot over it, so the wick hangs in the water but the bottom of the pot never touches it.
data.comment: Guide, watering through a wick: step 4.

data.name: Wick_Step5
data.value: Many growers water once from the top to settle the mix around the roots.
data.comment: Guide, watering through a wick: step 5.

data.name: Wick_GrowsIn
data.value: What it grows in
data.comment: Guide, watering through a wick: label over the choice of what it grows in.

data.name: Wick_Soil
data.value: Soil
data.comment: Guide, watering through a wick: name of a method.

data.name: Wick_SemiHydro
data.value: Semi-hydro
data.comment: Guide, watering through a wick: name of a method.

data.name: Wick_SoilWhy
data.value: The plant stays in soil and simply gets its water from below.
data.comment: Guide, watering through a wick, soil: why people pick it.

data.name: Wick_SoilMix
data.value: An ordinary potting mix stays too wet. Wick growers open it up with a lot of perlite, often half the mix or more.
data.comment: Guide, watering through a wick, soil: the mix.

data.name: Wick_SoilWatch
data.value: The top of the mix staying dry on a plant with few roots. Water small plants and new cuttings from the top for a few weeks until the roots reach down.
data.comment: Guide, watering through a wick, soil: what to watch for.

data.name: Wick_SemiWhy
data.value: The pebbles never stand in the water, so the roots always have air, and a slow drinker is less likely to rot, as many growers see it.
data.comment: Guide, watering through a wick, semi-hydro: why people pick it.

data.name: Wick_SemiMix
data.value: LECA alone wicks poorly, since the round pebbles barely touch. Many growers use PON, pumice or perlite, or mix some into the LECA.
data.comment: Guide, watering through a wick, semi-hydro: the mix.

data.name: Wick_SemiWatch
data.value: A dry top layer. Roots that grow out through the hole into the water are fine, say many growers.
data.comment: Guide, watering through a wick, semi-hydro: what to watch for.

data.name: Wick_CareTitle
data.value: Looking after it
data.comment: Guide, watering through a wick: heading.

data.name: Wick_Care1
data.value: Fill the container before it runs dry. A dry wick stops drawing and has to be wetted again.
data.comment: Guide, watering through a wick: looking after it.

data.name: Wick_Care2
data.value: Liquid feed can go in the water. Many growers use it weaker than on the bottle, since it goes in every time.
data.comment: Guide, watering through a wick: looking after it.

data.name: Wick_Care3
data.value: Water from the top now and then, which flushes out salts that build up when water only comes from below. Many growers do.
data.comment: Guide, watering through a wick: looking after it.

data.name: Wick_Care4
data.value: Keep light off the water, or it grows algae. The colour of the wick doesn't matter.
data.comment: Guide, watering through a wick: looking after it.

data.name: Wick_Care5
data.value: Many growers change the wick if it goes slimy or stops drawing.
data.comment: Guide, watering through a wick: looking after it.

data.name: Wick_DisagreeTitle
data.value: Where growers disagree
data.comment: Guide, watering through a wick: heading.

data.name: Wick_Disagree1
data.value: Wick or no wick in semi-hydro: some growers wick every pot, others take the wicks out and let the pebbles stand in a shallow layer of water instead.
data.comment: Guide, watering through a wick: where growers disagree.

data.name: Wick_Disagree2
data.value: How thick: some growers split a yarn into single strands for small pots. One careful source says thickness only changes how fast the water comes, not how wet the mix is.
data.comment: Guide, watering through a wick: where growers disagree.

data.name: Wick_InApp
data.value: A pot can be marked as a self-watering pot with a wick on the Pots page, and the watering reminder then learns how long the water lasts instead of how long the soil takes to dry.
data.comment: Guide, watering through a wick: how it works in the app.

data.name: Wick_Where
data.value: No RHS or extension page covers wick pots for houseplants beyond a mention in one old Cornell paper. The most careful page found leans on research for how wet a mix stays, one source is a pot maker, and the rest is what growers do.
data.comment: Guide, watering through a wick: why the sources are thin. Shown under the lead.

data.name: Mix_Lead
data.value: A potting mix is a base that holds water with something added for air. Roots need both, and how much of each depends on the plant. Compost also breaks down and packs tighter over time, which is why plants are moved into fresh mix every couple of years.
data.comment: Guide, mixing soil: the lead paragraph.

data.name: Mix_Water
data.value: Many growers match the mix to how they water: a mix that drains fast suits someone who waters often, and one that holds more suits someone who waters less often.
data.comment: Guide, mixing soil: matching the mix to how you water.

data.name: Check_Lead
data.value: Most pests come into a home on a new plant, since many of them barely move on their own. Finding them early, while there are few, makes them much easier to deal with.

data.name: Check_NewTitle
data.value: New plants

data.name: Check_NewStep1
data.value: Look a plant over before you buy it or bring it home: the undersides of the leaves, where leaves meet the stem, the base, any flowers, and the roots, by sliding it out of its pot.

data.name: Check_NewStep2
data.value: Keep it away from your other plants for a while, at least a month where you can, so eggs have time to hatch and show.

data.name: Check_NewStep3
data.value: Look it over every week for the first several weeks. If nothing shows, once a month is enough.

data.name: Check_NewStep4
data.value: Look again at a plant that comes back in from outdoors.

data.name: Check_HowTitle
data.value: How to look

data.name: Check_How1
data.value: Turn the leaves over. Most pests sit on the undersides and where leaves meet the stem.

data.name: Check_How2
data.value: A magnifier that enlarges 10 times shows mites and eggs you can't see otherwise.

data.name: Check_How3
data.value: Shake a shoot over a sheet of white paper. Specks that walk are mites or thrips.

data.name: Check_How4
data.value: Sticky leaves, or a black film on them, mean something is sucking the sap above. The film is sooty mould growing on the sugary droppings, and wipes off with a damp cloth.

data.name: Check_TrapsTitle
data.value: Sticky traps

data.name: Check_Traps
data.value: Yellow traps catch fungus gnats and whitefly, and blue ones catch thrips. They show what is there and whether the numbers go up or down, but they don't clear a plant, and they catch harmless insects too.

data.name: Check_WhichTitle
data.value: Which pest is it?

data.name: Check_WhichThrips
data.value: Silvery patches dotted with tiny black droppings.

data.name: Check_WhichMites
data.value: Fine pale speckles, and fine webbing in a bad case.

data.name: Check_WhichGnats
data.value: Small dark flies around the pots.

data.name: Check_WhichMealy
data.value: White cottony fluff in leaf joints and crevices.

data.name: Check_WhichScale
data.value: Small brown bumps along the veins and stems that don't move.

data.name: Check_WhichAphids
data.value: Clusters on new shoots and buds, and white cast skins.

data.name: Check_WhichWhitefly
data.value: Tiny white flies that rise from the leaves when the plant is touched.

data.name: Check_FoundTitle
data.value: Found something

data.name: Check_FoundStep1
data.value: Move the plant away from the others. Wash your hands after handling it.

data.name: Check_FoundStep2
data.value: Look over the plants that stood near it.

data.name: Check_FoundStep3
data.value: Remove fallen and dead leaves, which can carry pests and eggs.

data.name: Check_FoundStep4
data.value: A plant badly overrun, above all by mealybugs or scale, can be easier to replace than to clear.

data.name: Check_SprayTitle
data.value: Before you spray anything

data.name: Check_Spray1
data.value: Use only a product sold for houseplants, for that pest and that kind of plant, and follow its label.

data.name: Check_Spray2
data.value: Spray outdoors if you can, and cover the undersides of the leaves and the stems.

data.name: Check_Spray3
data.value: Try it on a few leaves a day or two first, to see that it doesn't mark them.

data.name: Check_Spray4
data.value: Not on a plant that is dry and thirsty, or above 32°C.

data.name: Check_Spray5
data.value: Soap and oil only kill what they touch, so it takes more than one round.

data.name: Check_EnemiesTitle
data.value: Natural enemies

data.name: Check_Enemies
data.value: Predatory mites and insects can be bought by mail for most pests. They breed best from about 21°C and in good light, need the pest there to feed on, and most sprays kill them. The RHS says to leave a day after soap or oil before letting them out.

data.name: Check_InApp
data.value: Settings can start quarantine when you add a bought, swapped or gifted plant. A check with nothing found can be logged from a plant's menu. When you find something, open a pest case for the plants it covers, and Today keeps track of the treatments.

data.name: Thrips_Lead
data.value: Thrips are slender insects up to about 2 mm long that feed on leaves and flowers. They are hard to see, so the damage is often what shows first.

data.name: Thrips_See1
data.value: Leaves that turn dull, then silvery on top, dotted with tiny black droppings.

data.name: Thrips_See2
data.value: Pale flecks and scars, and new leaves and buds that grow twisted.

data.name: Thrips_See3
data.value: Narrow insects, more often under the leaves: dark adults with fringed wings folded along the back, and paler young without wings.

data.name: Thrips_See4
data.value: To find them, shake a shoot over white paper and look with a magnifier.

data.name: Thrips_PhotoAdult
data.value: A western flower thrips on a flower. The bar is 1 mm.

data.name: Thrips_Mistaken
data.value: Spider mites speckle leaves too, but leave fine webbing and no black droppings.

data.name: Thrips_Back
data.value: A female lays up to about 100 eggs, one or two a day, in young leaves and buds. The young feed, then rest in the mix or in sheltered spots on the plant before they grow wings, where sprays don't reach them. A generation takes about 24 to 35 days, and indoors they breed all year.

data.name: Thrips_FirstStep1
data.value: Move the plant away from the others.

data.name: Thrips_FirstStep2
data.value: Cut off the worst leaves and any flowers with thrips in them.

data.name: Thrips_FirstStep3
data.value: Hang a blue sticky trap above or among the plants, to see how many there are and whether that falls.

data.name: Thrips_Rinse
data.value: Rinse and cut off

data.name: Thrips_RinseHow
data.value: Rinse the plant with water, the undersides too, and keep cutting off what is badly hit.

data.name: Thrips_RinseWatch
data.value: Young growing again from the mix and buds. Rinsing reaches only what is on the leaves.

data.name: Thrips_SoapHow
data.value: Insecticidal soap or horticultural oil, sprayed so it covers the buds, the shoot tips and the undersides of the leaves.

data.name: Thrips_SoapRound
data.value: It only kills what it touches, so it takes more than one round.

data.name: Thrips_SoapWatch
data.value: Marked leaves. Try it on a few leaves first.

data.name: Thrips_EnemiesWhat
data.value: The RHS lists predatory mites (Amblyseius, Hypoaspis and Macrocheles species) and the predatory bug Orius laevigatus, for under glass.

data.name: Thrips_EnemiesUc
data.value: UC IPM, writing about gardens, finds that bought predators rarely clear thrips on their own.

data.name: Thrips_EnemiesWatch
data.value: They need warmth, light and thrips to eat.

data.name: Thrips_ProductHow
data.value: A product sold for houseplants and for thrips, used as its label says.

data.name: Thrips_Over
data.value: Leaves silvered by thrips stay silver after the thrips are gone, so look at the new leaves. Many growers take clean new growth and an empty trap for some weeks to mean it is over.

data.name: Thrips_InApp
data.value: A thrips case starts at 5 days between treatments, which you can change. Count the trap on the case to see whether the catch falls week by week, and once you stop treating, the case is watched until it has been clean long enough.

data.name: Mites_Lead
data.value: Spider mites are tiny relatives of spiders, about half a millimetre long, that feed from the undersides of leaves. They do most harm in warm, dry rooms.

data.name: Mites_See1
data.value: Fine pale speckles on the top of the leaves, which can turn yellow or bronze before the leaves dry and drop.

data.name: Mites_See2
data.value: Fine silk webbing between leaves and stems in a bad case.

data.name: Mites_See3
data.value: Under the leaves, tiny oval mites, yellowish green with two dark spots, or orange red in winter and when crowded, with round eggs. A magnifier that enlarges 10 times helps.

data.name: Mites_See4
data.value: Shake a shoot over white paper. Specks that walk are mites.

data.name: Mites_PhotoMite
data.value: A spider mite in its red form, with strands of silk.

data.name: Mites_PhotoWebbing
data.value: Webbing in a bad case, here on a tomato.

data.name: Mites_Mistaken
data.value: Thrips speckle leaves too, but leave tiny black droppings and no webbing.

data.name: Mites_Back
data.value: From egg to adult takes about 12 days at 21°C and about 55 at 10°C, so a warm room speeds them up. Dust and a plant short of water make it worse. The damage often shows after the mites have built up.

data.name: Mites_FirstStep1
data.value: Move the plant away from the others, and look over the plants that stood near it.

data.name: Mites_FirstStep2
data.value: Cut off the worst leaves.

data.name: Mites_Rinse
data.value: Rinse and wipe

data.name: Mites_RinseHow
data.value: Rinse the leaves often, above all the undersides, and wipe off dust. UC IPM, writing about gardens, sprays a plant with mites at least once a day.

data.name: Mites_RinseMist
data.value: Misting and moist air help keep them down, but don't clear them on their own.

data.name: Mites_SoapHow
data.value: Insecticidal soap or horticultural oil, reaching the undersides of the leaves. UC IPM's houseplant note keeps this for when rinsing hasn't worked.

data.name: Mites_SoapRound
data.value: It only kills what it touches, so it takes more than one round.

data.name: Mites_SoapWatch
data.value: Marked leaves. Try it on a few leaves first, and not on a dry plant or above 32°C.

data.name: Mites_EnemiesWhat
data.value: Phytoseiulus persimilis is the predatory mite most used, and eats every stage. Amblyseius species, often A. californicus, do less against a heavy attack but can be let out early and last longer.

data.name: Mites_EnemiesWatch
data.value: They need mites to eat and die out without them.

data.name: Mites_ProductHow
data.value: A product sold for houseplants and for mites, used as its label says.

data.name: Mites_Stop
data.value: If they keep coming back or get worse, UC IPM says to throw the plant out, and the RHS says the same of a plant badly infested in late summer.

data.name: Mites_Over
data.value: Many growers look for no new speckles on new leaves, and nothing walking on the paper for some weeks.

data.name: Mites_InApp
data.value: A spider mite case starts at 4 days between treatments, which you can change. Mites don't fly into sticky traps, so the trap is behind a small link on the case.

data.name: Gnats_Lead
data.value: Fungus gnats are small dark flies, 3 to 4 mm long, that run over the mix and fly slowly around the pots. The adults don't harm plants. Their larvae live in the mix and mostly eat dead roots, rotting bits and fungi.

data.name: Gnats_See1
data.value: Small dark flies on the mix, on the plant and at the windows.

data.name: Gnats_See2
data.value: In the top of the mix, slender white larvae up to 6 mm long with shiny black heads, and slime trails in very wet pots.

data.name: Gnats_See3
data.value: To check for larvae, lay a piece of raw potato on the mix, cut side down, and look under it after a few days.

data.name: Gnats_PhotoTrap
data.value: A yellow sticky trap in a houseplant's pot, full of fungus gnats.

data.name: Gnats_PhotoGnat
data.value: An adult fungus gnat.

data.name: Gnats_HarmTitle
data.value: Does it harm the plant?

data.name: Gnats_Harm
data.value: Seedlings and soft cuttings can be harmed. A plant with a few years of roots rarely is. Many larvae in a wet mix rich in organic matter can stunt young plants, but a wilting houseplant is more often down to watering or root rot than to gnats.

data.name: Gnats_Mistaken
data.value: Shore flies look much the same but have short, bristly antennae.

data.name: Gnats_Back
data.value: Eggs laid on the mix hatch in a few days, and the larvae turn into adults in the mix. From egg to adult takes about 17 days at 24°C, and indoors they breed all year.

data.name: Gnats_FirstStep1
data.value: They breed in mix that stays wet. Letting the top of the mix dry between waterings, where the plant can take it, and emptying water left in saucers, cuts their numbers.

data.name: Gnats_FirstStep2
data.value: Clear dead leaves and rotting bits off the pots.

data.name: Gnats_FirstStep3
data.value: When you repot, use fresh houseplant compost rather than old, which can hold eggs and larvae, and keep open bags closed.

data.name: Gnats_FirstMix
data.value: A mix with perlite or sand in it drains faster and stays wet for less time. See

data.name: Gnats_Traps
data.value: Sticky traps

data.name: Gnats_TrapsHow
data.value: Yellow sticky traps, cut into squares and stuck in the pots, catch the adults.

data.name: Gnats_TrapsWatch
data.value: They cut the numbers but don't end it while larvae are in the mix, and they catch helpful insects too.

data.name: Gnats_Bti
data.value: Bacteria in the water

data.name: Gnats_BtiHow
data.value: Bti (Bacillus thuringiensis israelensis), watered into the mix, kills the larvae.

data.name: Gnats_BtiRepeat
data.value: It doesn't last indoors, so it is repeated about every 5 days.

data.name: Gnats_Nematodes
data.value: Nematodes

data.name: Gnats_NemaHow
data.value: Steinernema feltiae, tiny worms watered into the mix, which kill the larvae.

data.name: Gnats_NemaNeed
data.value: They need a moist mix and 16 to 32°C, can breed in the mix and last, and are sold by mail and keep only a short time.

data.name: Gnats_Mites
data.value: Predatory mites

data.name: Gnats_MitesHow
data.value: The RHS lists the mites Hypoaspis miles and Macrocheles robustulus and the rove beetle Atheta coriaria, put in the mix to eat eggs, larvae and pupae.

data.name: Gnats_MitesUc
data.value: UC IPM finds Hypoaspis mites do poorly in a single houseplant and doesn't suggest them for homes.

data.name: Gnats_NoSpray
data.value: No spray is listed: UC IPM says other insecticides are rarely needed against fungus gnats in a home.

data.name: Gnats_Over
data.value: Many growers look for no new flies on the trap for some weeks, and no larvae under the potato.

data.name: Gnats_InApp
data.value: A fungus gnat case starts at 7 days between treatments, which you can change. Count the trap on the case to see whether the catch falls week by week.

data.name: Mealy_Lead
data.value: Mealybugs are soft, oval insects up to 4 mm long, hidden under white wax, that suck sap in tight spots. Females hardly move, so they nearly always come in on a new plant.

data.name: Mealy_See1
data.value: White cottony fluff in leaf joints, leaf sheaths and other crevices, with insects or orange pink eggs under it.

data.name: Mealy_See2
data.value: Sticky leaves, and black sooty mould on them.

data.name: Mealy_See3
data.value: A plant that grows slowly, yellows and drops leaves.

data.name: Mealy_See4
data.value: Long-tailed mealybugs have two tail threads longer than the body.

data.name: Mealy_See5
data.value: Root mealybugs live on the roots, with white wax on them, and are usually only found when repotting.

data.name: Mealy_PhotoColony
data.value: Mealybugs on a clivia leaf.

data.name: Mealy_PhotoLong
data.value: A long-tailed mealybug on an orchid bud.

data.name: Mealy_Mistaken
data.value: Some scale insects lay eggs under white wax, and some aphids have a white waxy coat. The larvae of the mealybug ladybird, sold to eat them, look like large mealybugs.

data.name: Mealy_Back
data.value: Females lay 100 to 200 eggs over 10 to 20 days in a cottony sac, and the young grow up in about a month in summer, all year indoors. The wax keeps sprays off, and they hide where sprays don't reach, so no single treatment gets them all. The RHS says it is often impossible to get rid of them completely.

data.name: Mealy_FirstStep1
data.value: Move the plant away from the others.

data.name: Mealy_FirstStep2
data.value: Look for egg sacs on the pot, stakes and saucer, and remove dead leaves, which can carry eggs.

data.name: Mealy_Wipe
data.value: Wipe off

data.name: Mealy_WipeHow
data.value: Pick them off, or dab each one with a cotton bud dipped in rubbing alcohol (isopropyl, 70% or weaker). On a sturdy plant, a strong spray of water every few days washes off those in the open.

data.name: Mealy_WipeWatch
data.value: Try the alcohol on a small part of the plant a day or two before, since it can burn leaves, and keep it away from flames.

data.name: Mealy_Spray
data.value: Spray

data.name: Mealy_SprayHow
data.value: Insecticidal soap, horticultural oil or neem oil, sprayed onto the insects. They work best on the young, which have less wax.

data.name: Mealy_SprayAlcohol
data.value: For more than a few, UC IPM gives a spray of 10 to 25% rubbing alcohol in water, repeated weekly until they are gone.

data.name: Mealy_SprayWatch
data.value: Try it on a few leaves first.

data.name: Mealy_EnemiesWhat
data.value: The mealybug ladybird Cryptolaemus montrouzieri, and parasitic wasps such as Leptomastix, which only attacks citrus mealybug.

data.name: Mealy_EnemiesWatch
data.value: They need warmth and do best from May to September. The ladybird needs egg sacs to breed, so it is let out when there are many.

data.name: Mealy_ProductHow
data.value: A product sold for houseplants and for mealybugs, used as its label says. Products that go in the soil work less well against mealybugs than against other sap suckers.

data.name: Mealy_Stop
data.value: A badly infested plant is often better thrown out than treated again and again.

data.name: Mealy_Over
data.value: Many growers look for no new fluff for some weeks, looking in the crevices and at the roots when you repot.

data.name: Mealy_InApp
data.value: A mealybug case starts at 7 days between treatments, which you can change.

data.name: Scale_Lead
data.value: Scale insects settle on a leaf or stem, stop moving and grow a waxy or hard shell. They look like small bumps, which makes them easy to miss.

data.name: Scale_See1
data.value: Small, light brown bumps shaped like limpets on the stems and along the veins under the leaves. Brown soft scale is common on houseplants.

data.name: Scale_See2
data.value: Sticky, shiny leaves and black sooty mould on them.

data.name: Scale_See3
data.value: Yellowing leaves and poor growth.

data.name: Scale_See4
data.value: Tiny yellow or orange young that walk, before they settle.

data.name: Scale_See5
data.value: On ferns, scale can look like the spore clusters under the fronds.

data.name: Scale_PhotoFicus
data.value: Brown soft scale on a ficus leaf, shiny with honeydew.

data.name: Scale_PhotoSingle
data.value: One brown soft scale beside a leaf's vein.

data.name: Scale_SoftTitle
data.value: Soft and armoured

data.name: Scale_Soft
data.value: Soft scale is rounded, its shell is its body, and it makes sticky honeydew. Armoured scale is flat, its cover lifts off and leaves the insect behind, it makes no honeydew, and sprays reach it less well.

data.name: Scale_AliveTitle
data.value: Alive or dead?

data.name: Scale_Alive
data.value: Dead scales stay stuck to the plant. Squash a few: live ones leave a wet smear, dead ones don't. Clean new growth is the sign a treatment worked.

data.name: Scale_Back
data.value: The young spread and settle within a day or two, and indoors scale breeds all year, so every stage is there at once. Sprays mostly kill the young.

data.name: Scale_FirstStep1
data.value: Move the plant away from the others.

data.name: Scale_FirstStep2
data.value: Cut off stems and leaves that are covered.

data.name: Scale_Scrape
data.value: Scrape off

data.name: Scale_ScrapeHow
data.value: Scrape or wipe the adults off, and wash the young off with water.

data.name: Scale_ScrapeWatch
data.value: On a big plant this may not keep up.

data.name: Scale_SoapHow
data.value: Insecticidal soap or horticultural oil, which work best on the small young. Cover the plant well.

data.name: Scale_SoapRound
data.value: Since there are young all year indoors, it takes more than one round.

data.name: Scale_EnemiesWhat
data.value: For soft scale, parasitic wasps such as Metaphycus helvolus, and the nematode Steinernema feltiae. For armoured scale indoors, the ladybirds Chilocorus nigritus and Rhyzobius lophanthae.

data.name: Scale_ProductHow
data.value: A product sold for houseplants and for scale, used as its label says. One that goes in the soil works against some soft scales.

data.name: Scale_FewTitle
data.value: A few is fine

data.name: Scale_Few
data.value: A healthy plant copes with a few scale insects, so not every one has to go. One badly overrun can be easier to replace.

data.name: Scale_Over
data.value: New leaves and stems that stay clean for some weeks.

data.name: Scale_InApp
data.value: A scale case starts at 7 days between treatments, which you can change.

data.name: Aphids_Lead
data.value: Aphids are soft, pear-shaped insects, 1 to 7 mm long, green, black, yellow, pink or white, that live in colonies on new growth. Unlike most pests, they are easy to see.

data.name: Aphids_See1
data.value: Clusters on shoot tips, buds and under young leaves.

data.name: Aphids_See2
data.value: White cast skins on the tops of the leaves.

data.name: Aphids_See3
data.value: Sticky leaves, and black sooty mould on them.

data.name: Aphids_See4
data.value: New leaves that curl and twist.

data.name: Aphids_See5
data.value: Two small tubes sticking out from the back end, which no other pest has.

data.name: Aphids_Photo
data.value: Aphids on a stem.

data.name: Aphids_Mistaken
data.value: White specks on top of the leaves are cast aphid skins, not whitefly. Aphids with a white waxy coat can look like mealybugs.

data.name: Aphids_Back
data.value: Indoors they are mostly females that give birth to live young without mating, up to a dozen a day, and in warmth a newborn is an adult in about a week. Winged ones appear when a colony is crowded and fly to other plants. Even so, heavy damage to houseplants is uncommon.

data.name: Aphids_FirstStep1
data.value: Move the plant away from the others.

data.name: Aphids_FirstStep2
data.value: Look over the shoot tips of the plants near it.

data.name: Aphids_Squash
data.value: Squash and rinse

data.name: Aphids_SquashHow
data.value: Squash colonies with your fingers, rinse them off with water, and cut off tips that are covered.

data.name: Aphids_SquashMould
data.value: Sooty mould wipes off with a damp cloth.

data.name: Aphids_SoapHow
data.value: Insecticidal soap, horticultural oil or neem oil.

data.name: Aphids_SoapRound
data.value: They only kill the aphids they touch, so it takes more than one round.

data.name: Aphids_SoapWatch
data.value: Try it on a few leaves first, and not on a dry plant or above 32°C.

data.name: Aphids_EnemiesWhat
data.value: Lacewing larvae, the predatory midge Aphidoletes aphidimyza and parasitic wasps such as Aphidius.

data.name: Aphids_ProductHow
data.value: A product sold for houseplants and for aphids, used as its label says. UC IPM's houseplant note keeps one that goes in the soil for last.

data.name: Aphids_Over
data.value: Many growers look for no new colonies on the shoot tips for some weeks.

data.name: Aphids_InApp
data.value: An aphid case starts at 5 days between treatments, which you can change.

data.name: Whitefly_Lead
data.value: Whiteflies are tiny white winged insects, about 1.5 mm long, that rise in a cloud when the plant is touched. Their young are flat and sit still under the leaves.

data.name: Whitefly_See1
data.value: Small white flies that rise from the leaves.

data.name: Whitefly_See2
data.value: Under the leaves, flat, oval, creamy young that look like scale, and grey white eggs, often in a ring.

data.name: Whitefly_See3
data.value: Sticky leaves, and black sooty mould on them.

data.name: Whitefly_See4
data.value: Leaves that yellow and drop. Poinsettias often have them.

data.name: Whitefly_See5
data.value: Black young are dead, killed by a parasitic wasp.

data.name: Whitefly_PhotoAdults
data.value: Adult whiteflies on a squash leaf.

data.name: Whitefly_PhotoYoung
data.value: Young whiteflies and a ring of eggs on a leaf.

data.name: Whitefly_Mistaken
data.value: White specks on top of the leaves are more likely cast aphid skins.

data.name: Whitefly_Back
data.value: Each female lays over 200 eggs, without needing a male, and from egg to adult takes about three weeks at 21°C. Indoors they breed all year. They quickly stop dying from most sprays, apart from soap and oil.

data.name: Whitefly_FirstStep1
data.value: Move the plant away from the others.

data.name: Whitefly_FirstStep2
data.value: Remove the worst leaves.

data.name: Whitefly_Traps
data.value: Sticky traps

data.name: Whitefly_TrapsHow
data.value: A yellow sticky trap in each pot catches adults.

data.name: Whitefly_TrapsWatch
data.value: They show how many there are and cut the numbers somewhat, but don't clear a plant.

data.name: Whitefly_Rinse
data.value: Rinse

data.name: Whitefly_RinseHow
data.value: Wash the eggs and young off the undersides of the leaves with water.

data.name: Whitefly_SoapHow
data.value: Insecticidal soap or horticultural oil, covering the undersides of the leaves well, repeated, and best in the early evening.

data.name: Whitefly_SoapWatch
data.value: Not on a dry plant or above 32°C.

data.name: Whitefly_EnemiesWhat
data.value: The parasitic wasp Encarsia formosa, let out before there are many, since it doesn't work at once. The young it kills turn black, so you can see it working. The predatory mite Amblyseius andersoni eats the eggs.

data.name: Whitefly_Stop
data.value: UC IPM says a plant with a large infestation may be best thrown out.

data.name: Whitefly_Over
data.value: Many growers look for no adults rising and nothing new on the trap for some weeks.

data.name: Whitefly_InApp
data.value: A whitefly case starts at 5 days between treatments, which you can change. Count the trap on the case to see whether the catch falls week by week.

data.value: Aroids
data.comment: Name of a guide, in the list and as its heading.

data.value: Climbing, aerial roots and alocasias at rest
data.comment: Line under a plant group guide in the list of guides.

data.name: Aroids_Lead
data.value: Aroids are the arum family, more than 100 genera, with monstera, philodendron, alocasia, anthurium, pothos and peace lily among them. Most have a flower made of a spike inside a hood, but only a few grown indoors have showy ones. Many climb trees in the wild and root onto them as they go.

data.name: Aroids_Look1
data.value: Most do well when the compost dries a little between waterings. The RHS waits until the top has dried for philodendrons, until it is almost dry for monsteras, and until the top 5 cm is dry for alocasias.

data.name: Aroids_Look2
data.value: Yellowing leaves and a plant that collapses point to roots rotting in wet compost.

data.name: Aroids_Look3
data.value: Brown leaf edges point to dry air.

data.name: Aroids_Look4
data.value: Long stems with fewer, smaller leaves mean too little light. A monstera in low light makes leaves with fewer holes.

data.name: Aroids_Look5
data.value: Direct sun can scorch the leaves.

data.name: LookAt
data.value: What to look at
data.comment: Heading in a plant group guide.

data.name: Aroids_Mix1
data.value: An open mix that drains well. The RHS mixes 2 parts orchid compost with 1 part peat-free ericaceous compost for monsteras and philodendrons, and 3 parts peat-free compost with 1 part grit for alocasias. Iowa State uses an ordinary potting mix for philodendrons. See Mixing soil.

data.name: Aroids_Mix2
data.value: A pot only a few centimetres bigger than the root ball, since a much bigger one stays wet and rots the roots. They do well slightly pot-bound.

data.name: Aroids_Mix3
data.value: A heavy pot for a big climber or a large alocasia, which get top-heavy.

data.name: MixPot
data.value: Mix and pot
data.comment: Heading in a plant group guide.

data.name: Aroids_MossWhy
data.value: The stems can root into the moss, and a plant that climbs often makes bigger leaves, with more holes on a monstera.

data.name: Aroids_MossHow
data.value: Tie the stems to the pole and keep the moss moist, or the roots won't grow into it.

data.name: Aroids_MossWatch
data.value: A plant that outgrows the pole. Many growers add a piece on top before it does.

data.name: Aroids_StakeWhy
data.value: It holds the plant up without a pole to keep moist.

data.name: Aroids_StakeHow
data.value: Tie the stems on, and guide the aerial roots down into the pot, where they root and help hold the plant. Many growers say a plant with its aerial roots in the pot does fine without a moss pole.

data.name: Aroids_TrailWhy
data.value: Climbing kinds like heartleaf philodendron and pothos hang well from a basket or a shelf.

data.name: Aroids_TrailWatch
data.value: Trailing stems usually keep smaller leaves than climbing ones.

data.name: Aroids_Climb
data.value: Give it something to climb

data.name: Aroids_ClimbNote
data.value: Bushy kinds need no support. For climbers, all of these are common:

data.name: Aroids_MossPole
data.value: Moss pole
data.comment: Guide, aroids: name of the method MossPole.

data.name: Aroids_Stake
data.value: Stake or trellis
data.comment: Guide, aroids: name of the method Stake.

data.name: Aroids_Trail
data.value: Let it trail
data.comment: Guide, aroids: name of the method Trail.

data.name: Aroids_Aerial
data.value: The roots that grow from the stems are how the plant climbs in the wild. They can be left, guided onto a pole or into the pot, or cut off close to the stem, which doesn't harm the plant.

data.name: Aroids_AerialTitle
data.value: Aerial roots

data.name: Aroids_Winter
data.value: Alocasias rest in winter. Kept cooler and drier, but above 10°C, they may lose some of their leaves, which is normal, and grow new ones in spring. Wet compost while they rest rots the roots. Many growers find some lose every leaf and go back to a bare corm or rhizome, which can sit still for months before it grows again.

data.name: Aroids_WinterTitle
data.value: Winter rest for alocasias

data.name: Aroids_New1
data.value: Stem cuttings with a node, rooted in water or a mix. See Taking a cutting.

data.name: Aroids_New2
data.value: Offsets, the small plants at the base of a grown alocasia or a bushy philodendron, cut off with some root and potted on their own.

data.name: Aroids_New3
data.value: Pieces of an alocasia's rhizome, in late spring or early summer.

data.name: Aroids_New4
data.value: The small corms found around an alocasia's roots when it is repotted. Many growers start them in damp moss or perlite in a closed box somewhere warm.

data.name: NewPlants
data.value: Making new plants
data.comment: Heading in a plant group guide.

data.name: Aroids_Gloves
data.value: The sap irritates skin, and the plants are poisonous if eaten. Wear gloves when cutting them, and keep them away from children and pets.

data.name: GlovesTitle
data.value: Gloves
data.comment: Heading in a plant group guide.

data.name: GuidesFor
data.value: Guides:
data.comment: Label before the links to the pest guides at the end of Problems in a plant group guide.

data.name: Aroids_Problems
data.value: Mealybugs, spider mites and scale. Spider mites like dry air, which alocasias often get.

data.name: Problems
data.value: Problems
data.comment: Heading in a plant group guide.

data.name: Aroids_InApp
data.value: When an alocasia drops its leaves for winter, mark it Dormant on its page, so it shows as resting rather than dead. A corm, an offset or a cutting can be tracked as a propagation from its parent.

data.name: TitleBegonias
data.value: Begonias
data.comment: Name of a guide, in the list and as its heading.

data.name: RowBegonias
data.value: Keeping the leaves dry, and the kinds that root from a leaf
data.comment: Line under a plant group guide in the list of guides.

data.name: LinkBegonias
data.value: Guide to begonias
data.comment: Link to a plant group guide, next to the place it is about.

data.name: Begonias_Lead
data.value: Begonias grown indoors come in a few kinds that are looked after differently: cane begonias with tall, bamboo-like stems, often called angel wings; rhizomatous ones like rex begonias, which grow from a creeping stem and are kept for their leaves; fibrous-rooted ones with upright stems; and semi-tuberous ones sold in flower. Cane begonias are the easiest indoors.

data.name: Begonias_Look1
data.value: Brown leaf edges: dry air, or too warm.

data.name: Begonias_Look2
data.value: Rotting or dropping leaves: air that is too damp, too much water or too little light.

data.name: Begonias_Look3
data.value: Flower buds that drop: dry air or too little water.

data.name: Begonias_Look4
data.value: The RHS says most begonias brought to it were overwatered or kept in air that was too dry. Roots rot quickly in compost that stays wet. Many growers let a rex begonia dry until the pot feels light.

data.name: Begonias_Dry
data.value: Don't wet the leaves or the middle of a rex or other rhizomatous begonia, and don't mist the fibrous kinds. Air that is damp and still brings powdery mildew and grey mould, so give them air as well as humidity.

data.name: Begonias_DryTitle
data.value: Keep the leaves dry

data.name: Begonias_Humid
data.value: The RHS gives rex and rhizomatous begonias high humidity in summer and stands cane and fibrous ones on a tray of damp gravel. Many growers find cane begonias manage in ordinary room air, and keep the rex begonias for a humid spot.

data.name: Begonias_HumidTitle
data.value: Humidity

data.name: Begonias_Mix
data.value: Peat-free multipurpose compost for cane and fibrous begonias. Many growers keep them in a pot on the small side.

data.name: FieldFor
data.value: For
data.comment: Label in a method of a guide, before which plants it is for.

data.name: Begonias_LeafFor
data.value: Rex and other rhizomatous begonias.

data.name: Begonias_LeafHow
data.value: Take a firm, newly grown leaf and cut off its stalk. Cut through the main veins on the underside, about 2.5 cm apart, and lay the leaf flat on a sandy cutting mix with the cuts touching it, held down with pins or small stones. Water it, cover it with a bag or dome that doesn't seal tight, and keep it warm and bright, out of direct sun.

data.name: Begonias_LeafLong
data.value: Small plants appear at the cuts in 6 to 8 weeks. Pot them up once they have two or three leaves.

data.name: Begonias_StemFor
data.value: Cane and fibrous begonias.

data.name: Begonias_StemHow
data.value: A piece 7 to 10 cm long cut just below a node, rooted in a sandy cutting mix, or in water.

data.name: Begonias_DivisionFor
data.value: Rhizomatous begonias.

data.name: Begonias_DivisionHow
data.value: In spring, divide the rhizome so each piece has one or more growing points.

data.value: Leaf cuttings

data.name: Begonias_Stem
data.value: Stem cuttings
data.comment: Guide, begonias: name of the method Stem.

data.name: Begonias_Division
data.value: Division
data.comment: Guide, begonias: name of the method Division.

data.name: Begonias_Rest
data.value: Semi-tuberous begonias rest for about six weeks after flowering, cooler and with less water, then are cut back. Rex and cane begonias only get less water in winter.

data.name: RestTitle
data.value: Rest
data.comment: Heading in a plant group guide.

data.name: Begonias_Problems
data.value: Aphids and spider mites, and powdery mildew and grey mould.

data.name: Begonias_InApp
data.value: A leaf cutting can be tracked as a propagation of the kind Leaf, and a bag or dome as a rooting aid, so the results page shows whether it helped.

data.name: TitleBrom
data.value: Bromeliads and air plants
data.comment: Name of a guide, in the list and as its heading.

data.name: RowBrom
data.value: The cup, pups, and air plants that need no soil
data.comment: Line under a plant group guide in the list of guides.

data.name: LinkBrom
data.value: Guide to bromeliads and air plants
data.comment: Link to a plant group guide, next to the place it is about.

data.name: Brom_Lead
data.value: Bromeliads grow as a rosette of leaves, and many hold water in a cup in the middle. Air plants (Tillandsia) are bromeliads too, and most live with no compost at all. They take up water and food mainly through their leaves and the cup, and the roots mostly hold the plant in place.

data.name: Brom_Look1
data.value: Long, thin, greener leaves mean too little light, and shorter, thicker, paler ones a lot. Bleached or brown patches are scorch from strong sun.

data.name: Brom_Look2
data.value: Brown leaf tips and rotting roots: too much water, or a pot standing wet.

data.name: Brom_Look3
data.value: An air plant whose middle or leaves turn brown or black is rotting, mostly from water left in the middle with too little air around it.

data.name: Brom_Look4
data.value: An air plant that dries out was watered too seldom, too warm or in too dry air. An overnight soak can sometimes bring it back. Many growers say the leaves curl more when it is dry.

data.name: Brom_Cup
data.value: Keep the cup in the middle filled, with rainwater or distilled water if you can, and empty it and fill it fresh every month or two so it doesn't go stale. Keep the compost damp but not wet. Fresh water in the cup also keeps mosquito larvae out.

data.name: Brom_CupTitle
data.value: The cup

data.name: Brom_Mix
data.value: A loose mix, like equal parts fine bark, grit and coir, or peat, bark and coarse sand. Most need only a small pot, 7.5 to 12.5 cm.

data.name: Brom_Air1
data.value: No compost. Fix them to wood, shells or stone with wire, a tie or glue.

data.name: Brom_Air2
data.value: Rainwater. Hard tap water leaves a crust on the small scales that take up water.

data.name: Brom_Air3
data.value: Let them dry after watering, turned upside down or shaken, so no water sits in the middle. Many growers make sure they are dry within a few hours.

data.name: Brom_Air4
data.value: Not below 12°C.

data.name: Brom_AirTitle
data.value: Air plants

data.name: Brom_SoakWhy
data.value: The whole plant gets wet at once. The RHS waters this way.

data.name: Brom_SoakHow
data.value: Put the plant under rainwater for a while, then let it dry. Many growers soak for 20 to 30 minutes.

data.name: Brom_SoakWatch
data.value: Water left in the middle. Some growers find the thick, silvery kinds, like xerographica, rot from soaking.

data.name: Brom_MistWhy
data.value: Less water stays in the middle. Some growers mist the silvery kinds rather than soak them.

data.name: Brom_MistHow
data.value: Mist the whole plant. The RHS mists only between soaks, in warm weather, and says misting alone is not enough.

data.name: Brom_Watering
data.value: Watering an air plant

data.name: Brom_Soaking
data.value: Soaking
data.comment: Guide, bromeliads: name of the method Soaking.

data.name: Brom_Misting
data.value: Misting
data.comment: Guide, bromeliads: name of the method Misting.

data.name: Brom_Flowers
data.value: The colourful part is a bract that lasts for months. Most bromeliads flower only once and then slowly die, after making pups at the base. A grown bromeliad that won't flower can be put in a large clear bag with a few ripe apples or bananas for up to two weeks.

data.name: Brom_FlowersTitle
data.value: Flowers and pups

data.name: Brom_New
data.value: Cut a pup off once it is about a third the size of its parent, in spring, and pot it up or treat it as a grown air plant. With only one pup, the old rosette can be cut away after flowering instead.

data.name: Brom_Problems
data.value: Mealybugs and scale.

data.name: Brom_InApp
data.value: A pup with its own roots is a plant: add it with its parent picked. Before that it can be tracked as a propagation of the kind Offset. The flowering log under More on the plant's page keeps when it flowered.

data.name: TitleSucc
data.value: Cacti and succulents
data.comment: Name of a guide, in the list and as its heading.

data.name: RowSucc
data.value: Light, a gritty mix, winter rest and stretched plants
data.comment: Line under a plant group guide in the list of guides.

data.name: LinkSucc
data.value: Guide to cacti and succulents
data.comment: Link to a plant group guide, next to the place it is about.

data.name: Succ_Lead
data.value: Cacti and succulents store water in thick leaves or stems. They need a lot of light, a mix that drains fast and compost that dries between waterings.

data.name: Succ_Look1
data.value: Wrinkled or drying lower leaves, or a shrivelling plant: too dry.

data.name: Succ_Look2
data.value: Yellowing leaves, soft stems, blisters or rot: too wet.

data.name: Succ_Look3
data.value: Pale, stretched growth that leans to the window: too little light. Turning the pot keeps it even.

data.name: Succ_Look4
data.value: Wait until the compost is dry before watering, then water so it runs out of the bottom, and never leave the pot standing in water.

data.name: Succ_Look5
data.value: A white, chalky crust on the leaves comes from hard tap water. The RHS uses rainwater.

data.name: Succ_Forest
data.value: Christmas cactus, orchid cactus (Epiphyllum) and Rhipsalis like semi-shade, an east or west window, and more water than other cacti. A Christmas cactus flowers in winter and rests in summer.

data.name: Succ_ForestTitle
data.value: Forest cacti are different

data.name: Succ_Mix1
data.value: A gritty mix: a ready-made cactus compost, or loam-based compost with up to 30% grit. Iowa State uses 1 part potting soil, bark or coir to 2 parts perlite, sand, pumice or gravel. See Mixing soil.

data.name: Succ_Mix2
data.value: A pot with a hole in the bottom, only just big enough. Clay dries faster.

data.name: Succ_Mix3
data.value: Hold a spiny plant with a band of folded newspaper or thick gloves.

data.name: Succ_Rest
data.value: Most rest from November to early March. The RHS keeps them at 8 to 10°C at night and gives them only enough water to stop them shrivelling, and a cool, dry, bright rest helps them flower.

data.name: Succ_RestTitle
data.value: Winter rest

data.name: Succ_Stretch
data.value: A plant that has stretched stays stretched. Many growers cut off the top, let it dry, root it as a cutting, and leave the stem, which often grows new heads.

data.name: Succ_StretchTitle
data.value: Stretched plants

data.name: Succ_OffsetsFor
data.value: Kinds that grow in clumps or rosettes, like aloe.

data.name: Succ_OffsetsHow
data.value: Cut off an offset once it has roots of its own, and pot it up. Many growers wait until it is about a third the size of the plant, and let the cut dry for a few days first.

data.name: Succ_StemFor
data.value: Branching plants and columnar cacti.

data.name: Succ_StemHow
data.value: Cut a piece of stem, leave it to dry and seal for a day to a week, then set it in a gritty mix kept only just moist.

data.name: Succ_StemLong
data.value: Roots in a few weeks to a month. A gentle tug that meets resistance means roots.

data.name: Succ_LeavesFor
data.value: Many succulents, like echeveria and crassula. Many growers find that aloe, haworthia and the string-of plants rarely or never grow from a single leaf.

data.name: Succ_LeavesHow
data.value: Let a leaf dry like a cutting and lay it on the mix. Many growers twist it off whole, so it breaks cleanly where it met the stem.

data.name: Succ_LeavesLong
data.value: A small plant forms at the base in one to two months, and the old leaf shrivels away.

data.name: Succ_SeedHow
data.value: Sow in spring on a gritty mix, cover small seeds only with sand, keep it at about 21°C, bright but out of direct sun, under glass or a clear bag. Seedlings can take up to a year to be big enough to pot.

data.name: Succ_Problems
data.value: Mealybugs, spider mites and scale. Cold causes dead or discoloured patches.
