data.name: TitleCarniv
data.value: Carnivorous plants
data.comment: Name of a guide, in the list and as its heading.

data.name: RowCarniv
data.value: Water without minerals, a poor mix, food and a winter rest
data.comment: Line under a plant group guide in the list of guides.

data.name: LinkCarniv
data.value: Guide to carnivorous plants
data.comment: Link to a plant group guide, next to the place it is about.

data.name: Carniv_Lead
data.value: Carnivorous plants grow in bogs and other places too poor for most plants, and catch insects for what the soil lacks. The easiest indoors are the Cape sundew, the Venus flytrap and the purple pitcher plant. Tropical pitcher plants (Nepenthes) need warmth and humid air.

data.name: Carniv_Water
data.value: Rainwater, distilled water or reverse osmosis water. Tap water can kill them, above all hard water. The ICPS uses tap water only when it has under 90 ppm of dissolved salts, and says an ordinary water filter doesn't take them out.

data.name: WaterTitle
data.value: Water
data.comment: Heading in a plant group guide.

data.name: Carniv_Standing
data.value: Most stand in a saucer of water while they grow. The RHS keeps up to 2.5 cm in it, and the ICPS keeps the water at least 5 cm below the surface of the mix. In winter the RHS waters from below and tips the rest away.

data.name: Carniv_StandingTitle
data.value: Standing in water

data.name: Carniv_Mix1
data.value: A mix with almost no food in it, never potting compost or garden soil, and no fertiliser.

data.name: Carniv_Mix2
data.value: The ICPS uses peat and sand 1 to 1, or pure sphagnum, and no perlite. The RHS avoids peat and uses sphagnum with fine pine bark.

data.name: Carniv_Mix3
data.value: Keep a new plant in its pot and mix for the first year.

data.name: Carniv_Food1
data.value: Most catch enough on their own. Indoors, where there is little to catch, the ICPS feeds flytraps live insects or soaked dried bloodworms.

data.name: Carniv_Food2
data.value: A trap only digests something that moves, so a dead insect needs the trap gently pressed after it closes.

data.name: Carniv_Food3
data.value: A flytrap's trap closes only a few times before it dies, so don't set them off for fun.

data.name: Carniv_FoodTitle
data.value: Food

data.name: Carniv_Light
data.value: The RHS keeps them bright but out of direct sun behind glass, which can scorch them. A flytrap in poor light makes weak traps, and in strong light they turn red. The ICPS finds a windowsill too dark for a flytrap and grows them under lights. Pitcher plants with thick, waxy leaves do well in a window with some direct sun.

data.name: Carniv_LightTitle
data.value: Light

data.name: Carniv_RestWhy
data.value: The RHS gives flytraps and many other carnivorous plants a rest in winter.

data.name: Carniv_RestHow
data.value: A cooler spot in winter, not a warm room, but above 10°C indoors, and less water, given only when the mix starts to dry. Some lose leaves.

data.name: Carniv_GrowWhy
data.value: The ICPS has grown flytraps indoors under lights for years without a rest, and says one is only needed for plants outdoors that freeze. Many growers do the same, and others still give a rest.

data.name: Carniv_GrowHow
data.value: Under lights on a timer, kept the same all year.

data.name: Carniv_GrowWatch
data.value: A rest in the fridge for a plant indoors does nothing, the ICPS says.

data.name: Carniv_Winter
data.value: Winter for a flytrap

data.name: Carniv_Rest
data.value: A cool rest
data.comment: Guide, carnivorous-plants: name of the method Rest.

data.name: Carniv_GrowOn
data.value: Growing on
data.comment: Guide, carnivorous-plants: name of the method GrowOn.

data.name: Carniv_Tropical
data.value: Many growers say tropical pitcher plants don't rest at all.

data.name: Carniv_Flowers
data.value: The RHS cuts off flowers once they fade. Many growers let flytraps flower and say it doesn't kill them.

data.name: FlowersTitle
data.value: Flowers
data.comment: Heading in a plant group guide.

data.name: Carniv_New1
data.value: Flytraps: divide a large clump with four or more crowns.

data.name: Carniv_New2
data.value: Sundews and butterworts: leaf cuttings, division or seed.

data.name: Carniv_New3
data.value: Tropical pitcher plants: stem cuttings.

data.name: Carniv_New4
data.value: Trumpet pitchers: divide large clumps, or rhizome cuttings.

data.name: Carniv_Problems
data.value: Aphids and mealybugs on new shoots, and grey mould indoors. Most problems go away with the right water and mix. A few sundews among other plants catch fungus gnats.

data.name: Carniv_InApp
data.value: For a flytrap given a rest, set the growing season to Rests in winter, kept cooler, and Today asks "Gone dormant?" when it comes round.

data.name: TitleFerns
data.value: Ferns
data.comment: Name of a guide, in the list and as its heading.

data.name: RowFerns
data.value: Humid air, brown fronds and spore cases
data.comment: Line under a plant group guide in the list of guides.

data.name: LinkFerns
data.value: Guide to ferns
data.comment: Link to a plant group guide, next to the place it is about.

data.name: Ferns_Lead
data.value: The ferns kept indoors are ones that can't take temperatures below 10°C. Some grow in the ground, like Boston and maidenhair ferns. Others grow on trees in the wild, like bird's nest, hare's foot and staghorn ferns, and need less water than ground ferns. Tough, leathery ferns manage indoor air better than fine, feathery ones.

data.name: Ferns_Look1
data.value: Brown fronds can come from too much water, hard tap water, direct sun, dry air, a cold draught or a radiator. Check the compost first: brown often means less water, not more.

data.name: Ferns_Look2
data.value: Brown leaflets on fine fronds, like a maidenhair's, mean dry air.

data.name: Ferns_Look3
data.value: Ground ferns should never dry out completely. The tree-growing kinds are watered once the compost starts to feel dry.

data.name: Ferns_Look4
data.value: Rows of brown dots under the fronds are spore cases, part of the fern. Scale insects can look like them.

data.name: Ferns_PhotoSori
data.value: The spore cases (sori) on the underside of the fronds of Nephrolepis cordifolia.
data.comment: Guide, ferns: caption of a photo.

data.name: Ferns_Humid
data.value: A tray of damp gravel under the pot, plants grouped together, a bright bathroom or a glass case. Clemson stands the pot inside a bigger one lined with damp sphagnum. Indoor air is driest in winter.

data.name: HumidAirTitle
data.value: Humid air
data.comment: Heading in a plant group guide.

data.name: Ferns_Water
data.value: Rainwater or filtered water where you can, at room temperature. Hard tap water undoes the slightly acid mix they like.

data.name: Ferns_Mix1
data.value: An open, slightly acid mix: the RHS uses 2 parts peat-free ericaceous compost, 1 part perlite and 1 part orchid bark, or orchid compost alone for many tree-growing kinds.

data.name: Ferns_Mix2
data.value: Repot in spring once the roots are crowded, into a pot just bigger than the roots. Don't bury the furry surface stems of a hare's foot fern.

data.name: Ferns_Mix3
data.value: A staghorn fern grows on a board or bark, not in soil, held on by the round, flat fronds at its base. It needs very humid air.

data.name: Ferns_New1
data.value: Divide a clump so each part has plenty of fronds and roots, cutting a tight root ball if needed.

data.name: Ferns_New2
data.value: Ferns with creeping stems, like hare's foot ferns, can be divided along the stem.

data.name: Ferns_New3
data.value: From spores, which is possible but hard.

data.name: Ferns_Problems
data.value: Scale insects and mites are the most common, and Boston ferns also get mealybugs. Many sprays harm ferns, so try one on a small part first. Pests can often be picked off or rinsed off with water.

data.name: Ferns_InApp
data.value: A division with its own roots can be added straight away as a plant with its parent picked.

data.name: TitleHoyas
data.value: Hoyas
data.comment: Name of a guide, in the list and as its heading.

data.name: RowHoyas
data.value: Watering by the leaves, peduncles and rooting a cutting
data.comment: Line under a plant group guide in the list of guides.

data.name: LinkHoyas
data.value: Guide to hoyas
data.comment: Link to a plant group guide, next to the place it is about.

data.name: Hoyas_Lead
data.value: Hoyas, or wax plants, are climbing and trailing plants with thick leaves, from tropical Asia and Australia. Many grow on trees in the wild. They flower in clusters of waxy, often scented stars.

data.name: Hoyas_Look1
data.value: Thick leaves hold a lot of water. Collectors wait until the leaves pucker slightly before watering. Wrinkled or soft leaves mean dry, but soft leaves in wet compost can mean damaged roots.

data.name: Hoyas_Look2
data.value: Yellow leaves in compost that stays wet: too much water.

data.name: Hoyas_Look3
data.value: Thin, stretched growth and no flowers: too little light. Leaves that redden or scorch: too much.

data.name: Hoyas_Look4
data.value: Leaves that drop or blacken, and stems that die back, come from waterlogged compost or a cold winter. A plant with rotting roots seldom recovers, so take cuttings as soon as you see it.

data.name: Hoyas_Mix1
data.value: A chunky mix that drains at once, like equal parts orchid bark, peat-free compost and coarse perlite, or potting soil with bark and perlite or pumice. Many growers use a mostly bark mix in a clear pot.

data.name: Hoyas_Mix2
data.value: A snug pot. Hoyas flower better slightly pot-bound, and a big pot stays wet. Move up only one size, when the roots fill the pot.

data.name: Hoyas_Mix3
data.value: A wire hoop, a trellis or a hanging pot.

data.name: Hoyas_Flowers1
data.value: Hoyas flower from short spurs called peduncles, and many flower from the same one again and again. Don't cut them off with the old flowers.

data.name: Hoyas_Flowers2
data.value: Once buds show, don't move or turn the plant, since a change of light or water drops them.

data.name: Hoyas_Flowers3
data.value: Young plants often take several years to flower. A plant that grows well but doesn't flower usually needs more light.

data.name: Hoyas_PhotoPeduncle
data.value: The old flower peduncle of a Hoya carnosa, still on the stem.
data.comment: Guide, hoyas: caption of a photo.

data.name: Hoyas_Rest
data.value: From October to February they grow little. The RHS keeps them a bit cooler and drier then, but never dry right through.

data.name: Hoyas_Pruning
data.value: Light pruning only, in late winter or early spring. Hoyas don't take hard pruning.

data.name: Hoyas_PruningTitle
data.value: Pruning

data.name: Hoyas_WaterHow
data.value: Stand it with the node in water.

data.name: Hoyas_WaterLong
data.value: Roots in two or three weeks.

data.name: Hoyas_SphagnumHow
data.value: The node in damp sphagnum. Some growers wrap moss round each node, lay the cuttings on a damp mix and close them in a clear bag.

data.name: Hoyas_MixHow
data.value: A light propagation mix. Many growers use perlite, which makes the move to a pot easy.

data.name: Hoyas_Root
data.value: Root a cutting in

data.name: Hoyas_RootNote
data.value: Take a piece with one or two nodes and take off the lowest leaves. A single leaf roots, but never grows into a vine without a node at its base, which is how sweetheart hoyas are often sold.

data.name: Hoyas_Water
data.value: Water
data.comment: Guide, hoyas: name of the method Water.

data.name: Hoyas_Sphagnum
data.value: Sphagnum moss
data.comment: Guide, hoyas: name of the method Sphagnum.

data.name: Hoyas_LightMix
data.value: A light mix
data.comment: Guide, hoyas: name of the method LightMix.

data.name: Hoyas_Layering
data.value: A low shoot pegged down into a pot of cutting compost beside the plant, and cut free once it has rooted.

data.name: Hoyas_LayeringTitle
data.value: Layering

data.name: Hoyas_Gloves
data.value: The milky sap irritates skin.

data.name: Hoyas_Problems
data.value: Mealybugs, often hidden where the leaves meet the stem, scale, and spider mites, which come with very dry air.

data.name: Hoyas_InApp
data.value: The flowering log under More on the plant's page keeps when it budded and flowered, and after two years says when it usually starts.

data.name: TitleOrchids
data.value: Orchids
data.comment: Name of a guide, in the list and as its heading.

data.name: RowOrchids
data.value: Moth orchids: roots, watering, and what to do after they flower
data.comment: Line under a plant group guide in the list of guides.

data.name: LinkOrchids
data.value: Guide to orchids
data.comment: Link to a plant group guide, next to the place it is about.

data.name: Orchids_Lead
data.value: This guide is about moth orchids (Phalaenopsis), the easiest to grow at home and the ones sold most. In the wild their roots cling to trees in the open air. Other orchids, like slipper orchids, are looked after differently.

data.name: Orchids_Look1
data.value: The roots. Healthy roots are plump, firm and silvery white. Grey, shrivelled ones are too dry, and brown, mushy or hollow ones are dead. Many growers water once the roots turn from green to silvery.

data.name: Orchids_Look2
data.value: A clear pot shows the roots and the moisture inside.

data.name: Orchids_Look3
data.value: The weight of the pot: after a few waterings you can tell by lifting it. If in doubt, wait a day.

data.name: Orchids_Look4
data.value: The leaves: olive green is right. Darker means too little light, a red tinge too much.

data.name: Orchids_Water1
data.value: Never leave it standing in water, and blot any water left where the leaves meet in the middle, or it rots there.

data.name: Orchids_Water2
data.value: Use water at room temperature. The RHS uses rainwater or boiled water, since they don't like the chlorine in tap water. The American Orchid Society says not to use softened or distilled water.

data.name: Orchids_Water3
data.value: Bark holds less water than moss, so an orchid in moss needs water less often.

data.name: Orchids_Water4
data.value: Plain water now and then washes out the salts from feeding. Some growers water before they feed, since dry roots soak up the feed too strong.

data.name: Orchids_RunHow
data.value: In the sink, let tepid water run through the pot for a minute, then let it drain completely.

data.name: Orchids_SoakHow
data.value: Stand the pot in a bowl of water, then let it drain completely. Many growers soak for 15 to 30 minutes.

data.name: Orchids_How
data.value: How to water

data.name: Orchids_Run
data.value: Running water through
data.comment: Guide, orchids: name of the method Run.

data.name: Orchids_Soak
data.value: Soaking
data.comment: Guide, orchids: name of the method Soak.

data.name: Orchids_Ice
data.value: Ice cubes, sometimes sold with orchids, are not in any of these sources, and many growers advise against them.

data.name: Orchids_Mix1
data.value: Bark orchid compost. Never multipurpose or loam-based compost, which kills them.

data.name: Orchids_Mix2
data.value: Repot every one to three years, when the bark breaks down, while the roots have green tips. Cut off dead roots, set the plant at the same height and don't bury the roots growing in the air.

data.name: Orchids_Aerial
data.value: Roots growing above the pot are normal. Don't bury or cut them.

data.name: Orchids_AerialTitle
data.value: Aerial roots

data.name: Orchids_AfterLead
data.value: Both are common:

data.name: Orchids_After1
data.value: Cut the stem just above a node lower down, one of the small brown rings, and a side shoot often flowers again within 8 to 12 weeks.

data.name: Orchids_After2
data.value: Cut it down to the leaves. The plant flowers again within a year, with larger flowers on a stronger stem. If the stem turns pale and dry, cut it off at the base.

data.name: Orchids_AfterTitle
data.value: After it flowers

data.name: Orchids_Again
data.value: A healthy plant that hasn't flowered for a while can be moved somewhere about 5°C cooler for a month, or given more light. Cold draughts and changing temperatures make buds drop.

data.name: Orchids_AgainTitle
data.value: Flowering again

data.name: Orchids_Keikis
data.value: A keiki is a small plant that sometimes grows from a node on the flower stem. Once it has several good roots it can be cut off and potted in orchid compost.

data.name: Orchids_PhotoKeiki
data.value: A Phalaenopsis keiki, joined to the mother plant by the flower stem.
data.comment: Guide, orchids: caption of a photo.

data.name: Orchids_KeikisTitle
data.value: Keikis

data.name: Orchids_Problems
data.value: Mealybugs. Water on the flowers spots them.

data.name: Orchids_InApp
data.value: The flowering log under More on the plant's page keeps spikes, flowers and when it's done, and after two years says when it usually starts. A keiki with its own roots is a plant: add it with its parent picked.

data.name: TitlePrayer
data.value: Prayer plants
data.comment: Name of a guide, in the list and as its heading.

data.name: RowPrayer
data.value: Water, humid air and brown leaf edges
data.comment: Line under a plant group guide in the list of guides.

data.name: LinkPrayer
data.value: Guide to prayer plants
data.comment: Link to a plant group guide, next to the place it is about.

data.name: Prayer_Lead
data.value: Prayer plants are the arrowroot family: Maranta, and calatheas, most of which are called Goeppertia now. Their leaves fold up at night.

data.name: Prayer_Where
data.value: The RHS's calathea guide is the one full source. The rest is a short University of Illinois page, one extension answer and what growers say, and each part says which.

data.name: Prayer_Look1
data.value: Brown leaf tips and edges: dry air. Water with a lot of minerals or additives can cause them too.

data.name: Prayer_Look2
data.value: Patches that look soaked with water, mostly in winter: oedema, from compost kept too wet.

data.name: Prayer_Look3
data.value: Weak growth: too little light.

data.name: Prayer_Look4
data.value: Yellowing on the oldest, outermost leaves can be normal.

data.name: Prayer_Look5
data.value: Don't let water stand where the stems meet, since they rot easily.

data.name: Prayer_Water
data.value: Rainwater is best. Tap water left to stand for a day will do, and distilled water from a dehumidifier or tumble dryer works too. They react to hard water and to what is added to tap water. Many growers water with distilled or rainwater and say the brown edges stopped. Keep the compost evenly moist while they grow, and let the top dry a little in winter, but never dry through.

data.name: Prayer_Humid
data.value: A tray of damp gravel with the water below the top of the gravel, plants grouped together, or a bathroom. Sources differ on misting: the RHS mists the leaves regularly, and Maryland's answer says to stop, since wet leaves invite disease.

data.name: Prayer_Mix
data.value: A peat-free compost that holds water and drains, or multipurpose compost with about 10% grit. Repot every few years, one or two sizes up. Many growers check the root ball of a new plant for a mesh plug from the nursery.

data.name: Prayer_New1
data.value: Division in spring: cut the root ball into pieces with several leaves each, pot them on their own, and keep them warm, humid and moist until they grow.

data.name: Prayer_New2
data.value: Branching kinds like Ctenanthe: cut just below where a stem branches and root it in a covered pot.

data.name: Prayer_Problems
data.value: Spider mites, mealybugs and soft scale, and fungus gnats.

data.name: Prayer_InApp
data.value: For the common ones, the plant form offers the light, water and humidity they usually like.
